patient.chief_complaint: 2-year progressive triad: shuffling gait, urinary incontinence, and forgetfulness
patient.history_present_illness: A 73-year-old retired engineer with hypertension and hyperlipidemia was admitted for evaluation of a classic 2-year progressive triad: (1) Shuffling magnetic gait that has progressively worsened — he requires a cane and has had four falls in 6 months, including a hip bruise. His wife describes him as 'walking like his feet are glued to the floor.' (2) Progressive urinary urgency and incontinence — he wears pads daily and has nocturnal incontinence. (3) Progressive forgetfulness — his wife reports he frequently repeats himself, forgets recent conversations, and has become slow in decision-making. MMSE outpatient was 24/30. MRI obtained by his primary care physician shows 'significant ventriculomegaly' with reported Evans index 0.38. He was referred to neurology inpatient for tap trial. There is no prominent episodic amnesia isolated to encoding, no resting tremor or rigidity, and no orthostatic hypotension. All three symptoms began progressively over 2 years in a compatible timeframe.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented x4. MoCA 22/30 — loses primarily on trail-making, recall, and clock drawing. Frontal-subcortical pattern. No aphasia.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal tone and strength throughout. No tremor. No rigidity.
neurological_exam.sensory: Vibration mildly reduced at ankles (age-appropriate). Joint position intact.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-nose intact. Heel-shin mildly awkward bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Classic magnetic gait — short shuffling steps, wide base, markedly reduced foot clearance, en bloc turning requiring 8-10 steps. Gait freezing at doorways. TUG 28 seconds. 10-meter walk 22 seconds. Cannot tandem walk.
neurological_exam.additional: No cogwheel rigidity. No postural tremor. Pull test: 2 steps backward, recovers. No orthostatic hypotension on standing.

signal_characteristics.description: Classic tight high-convexity sulci with disproportionate sylvian fissure widening
Callosal angle 72 degrees on coronal imaging
Thinning and upward bowing of corpus callosum
Prominent aqueductal flow void on sagittal T1
Periventricular T2/FLAIR signal ('halo' of transependymal CSF seepage)

mri.impression: Ventriculomegaly with Evans index 0.38, callosal angle 72 degrees, DESH pattern, corpus callosum thinning and upward bowing, aqueductal flow void, and periventricular transependymal signal. Ventricular enlargement is disproportionate to the degree of cortical atrophy

Baseline workup.clinical_significance: Ordered as part of the baseline workup; no abnormality that alters the diagnosis, which is what this case's diagnosis rests on

special_tests.gait_description: Post-tap at 24h: markedly improved step height, longer steps, less freezing, better turns in 5-6 steps (vs 8-10 pre-tap)

csf.interpretation: Opening pressure: 12 cmH2O. WBC: 1 cell/mcL; RBC: 0. Protein: 38 mg/dL. Glucose: 66 mg/dL. Positive tap trial. TUG improved 36% at 24 hours (28 sec to 18 sec), 10-meter walk improved 32%, and MoCA improved 3 points (22 to 25). Gait improved in step height, stride length, and turn quality

scores.assessment timing: immediately before the large-volume tap, then repeated after it
scores.positive-response threshold: >10% TUG improvement is a commonly used criterion; interpret with absolute change and concordant gait/cognitive findings

pre_post_comparison.before the tap: Classic magnetic gait — short shuffling steps, wide base, markedly reduced foot clearance, en bloc turning requiring 8-10 steps.; Gait freezing at doorways.; Pull test: 2 steps backward, recovers.
pre_post_comparison.after the tap: The same measures were repeated after the tap, and this is what the case's own tap-trial report states: Positive tap trial. TUG improved 36% at 24 hours (28 sec to 18 sec), 10-meter walk improved 32%, and MoCA improved 3 points (22 to 25). Gait improved in step height, stride length, and turn quality.

findings.result: Classic magnetic gait — short shuffling steps, wide base, markedly reduced foot clearance, en bloc turning requiring 8-10 steps.

clinical_assessment.impression: Objective gait and cognition were measured before the large-volume tap and repeated after it. The objective improvement is consistent with a positive tap response and increases the likelihood of shunt responsiveness; it must be integrated with the clinical syndrome and structural imaging.

Grey-white differentiation preserved; basal cisterns patent.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic vascular disease
differential.key_features: Small-vessel disease can produce gait apraxia and executive slowing, but ventriculomegaly out of proportion to white-matter burden and a positive tap test favour NPH
Shuffling gait overlaps, but absence of resting tremor, asymmetric rigidity, or L-dopa response and presence of magnetic gait + DESH favour NPH

Cognitive decline overlaps; AD typically presents with episodic-memory predominance and hippocampal atrophy rather than frontal-subcortical pattern and magnetic gait; targeted CSF Alzheimer biomarkers can evaluate suspected copathology when the result would change counselling or management

differential.diagnosis: Cerebral atrophy with secondary ex-vacuo ventriculomegaly
differential.key_features: Ventriculomegaly proportionate to sulcal widening, callosal angle >90°, and absence of DESH or transependymal signal argue against true NPH
No history of trauma, SAH, or meningitis on review; would be considered if history suggested antecedent intracranial event

optimal_actions.action: Literature review of iNPH diagnostic criteria and shunt-response predictors
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Relkin 2005 INPH Study Group criteria; Tisell 2011 tap-test predictors; Williams 2016 review

optimal_actions.action: Brain MRI — measure Evans index, callosal angle, assess DESH pattern; exclude mass effect, hydrocephalus from secondary cause, and atrophy
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Ventriculomegaly with Evans index >0.3, DESH pattern (tight high-convexity sulci + widened Sylvian fissures), callosal angle <90°, periventricular transependymal signal; no mass effect or aqueductal obstruction

optimal_actions.action: Reversible-cause labs (TSH, B12, RPR, HIV) to exclude metabolic / infectious dementia mimics
optimal_actions.expected_finding: TSH, B12, RPR, HIV negative or within normal range; reversible mimics excluded

optimal_actions.action: Large-volume lumbar puncture (30-50 mL tap test) with opening pressure and prespecified pre/post objective gait and cognitive assessment
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Opening pressure compatible with NPH criteria; 30-50 mL CSF removed; prespecified pre/post gait and cognitive measures show objective change relevant to shunt responsiveness

optimal_actions.action: Neurosurgery consultation for VP shunt candidacy and perioperative planning
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Neurosurgery accepts patient for VP shunt evaluation with programmable valve

optimal_actions.action: Measure gait and balance objectively before the large-volume tap — timed-up-and-go, 10-metre walk, step length, falls risk — and repeat the same measures and the cognitive screen after it. The baseline must be recorded before the puncture or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Baseline timed gait recorded before the tap and repeated after it, with the response interpreted from the prespecified objective change and the cognitive screen repeated alongside

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is non-specific for NPH and does not distinguish from neurodegenerative alternatives in this chronic gait/cognitive presentation
ECG is unrelated to the diagnostic workup of chronic gait + cognitive + urinary triad once cardiogenic syncope is not on the differential
Echocardiography does not contribute to NPH evaluation in the absence of syncope or cardioembolic stroke workup
Head CT is inferior to MRI for measuring Evans index and callosal angle and for excluding secondary causes; only justified if MRI is contraindicated
Cardiac monitoring has no diagnostic role in NPH and is reserved for syncope or arrhythmia workup

sequence_constraints.reason: MRI must precede large-volume LP to exclude mass effect or secondary obstructive hydrocephalus before removing 30-50 mL of CSF
The baseline gait and cognition must be measured before the large-volume tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted and the tap test yields nothing

critical_actions: Obtain brain MRI before lumbar puncture to exclude mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus
Document objective pre-tap gait (TUG and 10-metre walk) and a brief cognitive baseline so that pre/post-tap change can be quantified
Remove 30-50 mL of CSF during the tap test (a low-volume LP under-samples and biases the test toward false negative)
Re-assess gait and cognition 1-4 hours after the tap and again at 24 hours (the response window for tap-test prediction of shunt benefit)
Refer to neurosurgery for VP shunt evaluation when imaging, clinical, and tap-test criteria support iNPH
contraindicated_actions: Do not perform large-volume lumbar puncture before MRI excludes mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus
Do not infer iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone — DESH, callosal angle <90°, and a clinical triad are required
Do not diagnose Alzheimer's disease in a patient with gait-predominant presentation and ventriculomegaly without first excluding NPH
Do not attribute the syndrome to 'normal ageing' or 'deconditioning' once the imaging criteria for ventriculomegaly are met
key_reasoning_points: iNPH diagnosis (Relkin 2005 INPH Study Group) requires (a) Hakim's triad of gait disturbance, cognitive impairment, and urinary urgency/incontinence — gait is typically first and most prominent; (b) ventriculomegaly with Evans >0.3 and DESH on MRI without mass effect; (c) age >40 and chronic course; (d) opening pressure <25 cmH2O; (e) absence of an alternative explanation
MRI is the imaging modality of choice — measure Evans index and callosal angle (<90° supports NPH) and confirm DESH (tight high-convexity sulci + wide Sylvian fissures)

The tap test removes 30-50 mL of CSF after measuring opening pressure and compares prespecified objective gait and cognitive measures before and after drainage; a positive response supports shunt responsiveness, while a negative single tap does not exclude NPH
Tap-test sensitivity is only 50-80%; a single negative tap does not exclude NPH — an extended (3-5 day) lumbar drainage trial can resolve borderline cases

Reversible-cause laboratory tests do not diagnose NPH and are optional; order targeted tests only when the presentation suggests a metabolic, endocrine, infectious, inflammatory, vitamin, or medication-related mimic
Alzheimer copathology is common in iNPH and may reduce cognitive benefit from shunting without necessarily eliminating gait benefit
Shunt response is best predicted by an objectively positive tap test or extended drainage trial in a patient who meets imaging and clinical criteria
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: The reversible-cause screen is good practice but does not establish or exclude hydrocephalus; the tap test does.
